newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Thomson-CSF sale halt draws fire.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Thomson-CSF sale halt draws fire.

text.p: Shares in Europe's top defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF tumbled on Tuesday as investors expressed doubts about the company's future after the government decided to halt its privatisation.

Recently-elected Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin cancelled the privatisation planned by his centre-right predecessors on Friday, saying it did not protect the interests of the state, the company or its employees.
Shares in 58-percent state-owned Thomson-CSF fell almost six percent in the market's first reaction following a long weekend. They moved off their lows to close 3.6 percent lower at 163.50 francs.

Shares in missiles-maker Lagardere, seen as the loser in a defence sector restructuring favouring a national French solution, dropped 2.23 percent to close at 175 francs. One analyst called the decision "a major blow" to Lagardere.

But engineering firm Alcatel Alsthom, which had bid against Lagardere in the just-cancelled privatisation, rose by slightly less than one percent to close at 772 francs, off its high of 790 francs reached earlier.
The stock was buoyed by weekend reports that despite halting the selloff, the government would link Alcatel to Thomson-CSF as a partner in a restructured French defence giant.

The daily Le Figaro said on Saturday that under the government's plan, the state would keep about 40 percent of the capital, Alcatel and other industrial partners would have 40 percent and the remaining 20 percent would be traded.
The government said on Friday it would maintain a "decisive" stake in Thomson-CSF in a new plan to be launched soon, but repeated on Tuesday that no decisions had been taken.

The share price action reflected a feeling widespread among analysts that despite the government's stated wish to smoothe a restructuring of the European defence industry, its first priority was a short-term protection of national sovereignty and jobs.
The move was condemned by defence sector analysts, who said it showed Jospin and his team fundamentally misunderstood the dynamics of the fast-changing global defence industry.
They added the decision could lead to the long-term decline of an already less robust French industry, squeezed by falling defence budgets and a series of U.S. mega-mergers.

"Industrially and financially we don't really understand the logic of this," said Emmanuel Dubois-Pelerin, analyst with Standard & Poor's in Paris. "They are favouring national and short-term interests rather than industrial and long-term interests. They think they can combine these two and I'm not sure they perceive the contradictions."
"You can't overstate the problems this is going to cause," said Paul Beaver, of Jane's Defence Weekly.

"This is a demonstration that the French are not interested in restructuring the European defence sector on commercial grounds," he said, adding the move sent a signal that France did not want an integrated defence industry because it wanted to maintain itsperceive dominace for "chauvinistic" reasons.

The analysts said the decision might backfire as a future French defence combine could face problems forging alliances with private companies in the rest of Europe if the government were seen to have too much control.

"The biggest obstacle the government has put in the way of CSF becoming a major and efficient player in the world industry is maintaining their presence in the company's capital," Dubois-Pelerin said.

Analysts said Thomson-CSF would still remain the "jewel in the crown" of the French defence sector and would continue to be a strong player, but that it could be even more efficient if the state released its shareholding.
"Though CSF is a good company with good market positions, there are many reasons to think they could be even more efficient and competitive if they were privatised," Dubois-Pelerin said.
The government has not said what it means by a "decisive" stake in Thomson-CSF, but has indicated it will keep a significant chunk of the company's equity in state hands.

Dubois-Pelerin said building a French defence giant from a combination of Thomson-CSF, Alcatel, warplane- maker Dassault Aviation and state-owned planemaker Aerospatiale -- one possibility for a national restructuring -- would result in an "extremely awkward" share structure.
